unit: One in-wheel tire pressure sensor (valve-stem type), fitted to one wheel: wheel off, tire bead broken, old sensor out, new sensor in, tire re-inflated, that wheel rebalanced, and the sensor programmed or relearned to the car. The stated times used here do not itemize what they cover: the Kia time is printed against "TPMS Sensor Replace One (1)" in a bulletin whose procedure includes the learning step, and the Ram seller figure is for a sensor that needs no programming and uses the truck's own relearn. Not included: the tire itself, valve-stem service kits for the other wheels, the other three sensors, and diagnosis of the warning light.

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. HELD: only two of the four classes have a stated one-sensor labor time. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): midsize 2016 Kia Optima about $135-$186 (0.7 hr); truck 2019 Ram 1500 about $171-$233 (1.0 hr); economy 2015 Kia Forte and luxury 2013 Land Rover LR4 not built (no one-sensor time; LR4 also has no priced part). The two built totals sit below RepairPal ($240-$299), CarParts.com ($250-$340 per wheel) and Kelley Blue Book ($314-$368) and inside J.D. Power ($50-$200 per tire) and PartCatalog ($120-$280 per sensor). Two reasons for the gap: the midsize labor figure is a Kia warranty time, which is the low end of what a shop bills, and our parts figures are single sensors at $51-$73 where RepairPal carries $164-$187 in parts. A supportable first range for a mainstream car or pickup is roughly $135-$235 per wheel, with benchmarks pointing to $240-$370 at dealer parts prices and a full minimum labor charge; it should not be published until the other classes are filled. How solid the labor times are: the Optima time (0.7 M/H for one sensor) is Kia's own figure for the example vehicle and is the best number in this file; Kia prints the same 0.7 for the 2016-2017 Sorento, and its tables show each extra sensor adding only 0.2, so most of the time is setup and the relearn, not the wheel. The Ram time is a parts seller's approximate one hour, not a book time; FCA's own allowance for all four sensors on Ram trucks is 1.4-1.5 hours, so one sensor at warranty pace is well under an hour. Whether the stated time includes programming: neither source itemizes it. Kia's procedure includes the sensor learning step; the Ram seller says its sensor needs no programming and uses the truck's own relearn. A programmable universal sensor that has to be cloned or configured with a TPMS tool can add a programming fee ($20-$80 per PartCatalog). Parts: no aftermarket page loaded states that its sensor is new, so every low end is a genuine sensor at an online discount and aftermarket prices ($24-$54) are recorded as cross-checks only; real quotes with an aftermarket sensor can be lower on parts than shown. What is missing and why: (1) economy hours: Kia prints only a four-sensor time for the 2014-2015 Forte (0.9 M/H); (2) luxury hours: Land Rover prints only four-wheel (1.60 hr) and five-wheel (2.0 hr) times; (3) luxury parts: no priced page for LR066378 was loaded; (4) economy parts rest on one page. Nissan, Honda, Acura, GM, Subaru and Infiniti TPMS bulletins loaded either print no time or refer to a labor-time manual. A second search round on 2026-11-20 did not change this. It found two more maker-stated one-sensor times, both recorded as cross-checks only because each includes an inspection of the sensors and neither is for an economy or luxury vehicle: Hyundai 0.7 M/H for "inspection and replacement (1 sensor)" on the 2017 Santa Fe Sport (inspection alone 0.3) and FCA 0.8 hours for "inspect and replace 1 TPMS and balance tires" on the 2022 Chrysler 300, Charger and Challenger (inspection alone 0.2). Together with Kia's 0.7 they put one sensor at warranty pace at about 0.7-0.8 hours on mainstream vehicles, which supports the midsize figure but does not fill the two missing classes. Kia bulletins for the 2014 Sportage and 2014 Sorento print only four-sensor times (0.9 and 1.0 M/H). To finish: find a one-sensor maker time, with no inspection folded in, for an economy car and a luxury car, load an aftermarket sensor price from a page that states the part is new and names the model year, and load a Land Rover or other luxury sensor price. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or TPMS scan fee to find which sensor has failed, a valve-stem service kit (seal, nut, core, cap) for each of the other wheels, a programming fee where a universal sensor has to be configured, shop supplies and sales tax. Sensor batteries are sealed in and tend to fail around the same age, so a shop will often recommend all four, which roughly quadruples the parts and adds a little labor per wheel. Doing the sensor while the tires are already off for new tires usually cuts the labor. A corroded stem that breaks on removal, or a spare-wheel sensor, adds to the bill.
held_reason: No stated one-sensor labor time for the economy and luxury classes (the makers print only four- or five-sensor times), no priced part for the luxury example, and one parts page for the economy example.
